6a971e9fa4a22c5817e2b574.implications: For a repo/rates desk this is core positioning input: front-end hawkish repricing (higher hike odds) alongside persistent long-end selling implies a steepening bias and higher term premium globally, with knock-on effects for funding costs, collateral yields, and cross-currency basis (US, UK, Japan, France all moving together); the AI-driven corporate bond issuance crowding out sovereign demand is also worth tracking as a technical driver of term rates.

6a971e9fa4a22c5817e2b574.one_liner: New Fed chair Kevin Warsh turned hawkish at Jackson Hole, market-implied odds of a September hike jumped from ~1-in-3 to ~2-in-3, yet long-end yields (US 10yr 4.8%, JGB 10yr 3%, UK highest since GFC) kept rising regardless -- a global term-premium/funding-cost story any rates or repo desk needs to track.
6a971e9fa4a22c5817e2b574.recap: Katie Martin and Rob Armstrong (FT Unhedged) review Fed chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech after two rocky press conferences in which he dropped forward guidance, mused about revisiting the 2% PCE inflation target, and said he was untroubled by rising borrowing costs -- all of which spooked bond markets and prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to publicly (and unsuccessfully) urge yields lower. At Jackson Hole, Warsh sharpened his message: employment is near full, inflation is too high and not improving, the Fed's only tool is rates, and the current inflation target is a "firm fixed target" he won't tinker with. He also dismissed slowing wage growth and the "no-hire-no-fire" labor market as signals of disinflation, calling the stagnant job market a post-COVID rematching effect rather than weakness. Markets read this as unambiguously hawkish: implied odds of a September Fed hike (rate cut context notwithstanding) moved from about one-in-three to two-in-thirds. Yet despite short-end hawkishness, long-end yields kept climbing globally -- US 10yr at 4.8%, Japan's 10yr hitting 3% for the first time since 1996, UK yields at post-financial-crisis highs, and France also under pressure. The hosts weigh competing explanations: Fed policy confusion, unanchored inflation expectations, strong nominal growth (~4% real growth plus ~3% inflation per Matt Klein's Overshoot newsletter), fiscal profligacy/oversupply of sovereign debt, and competition for capital from massive AI/hyperscaler bond issuance funding data centers. Bessent claims to have undisclosed plans regarding Japan/the yen. The episode closes noting equities have so far ignored the bond selloff, which the hosts flag as unusual and fragile.
